before.content_html:
What Was a Temple For?

When a Greek or Roman worshipper approached a temple, they were not entering a place of communal prayer in the way a modern churchgoer might. The cella — the inner room — was the private home of the god, accessible mainly to priests. Worshippers gathered outside at the altar, which stood in the open air in front of the east-facing entrance. The temple’s primary function was to provide a magnificent dwelling for the deity and to house the cult statue. Its grandeur was itself an act of worship, a visible statement of piety and civic pride.

Key Fact

A Greek temple typically consisted of three zones: the pronaos (entrance porch), the cella (inner chamber housing the cult statue), and sometimes an opisthodomos (rear porch, often used as a treasury). The altar stood outside the temple entirely, always to the east.

The Three Architectural Orders

Greek architects developed three distinct systems of design, each identified primarily by the style of its column and capital. The Doric order is the oldest and most austere. Its columns rise directly from the temple platform with no base, taper upward and are crowned by a plain, circular capital topped by a square slab. The overall effect is one of weight and power. The Ionic order is lighter and more elegant. Ionic columns stand on a moulded base, and their capitals are decorated with a pair of distinctive scroll-like spirals called volutes. The Corinthian order, rarely used on Greek temple exteriors but popular in the Roman world, features tall, slender columns and elaborately carved capitals decorated with acanthus leaves.

Greek architects generally used a single order throughout a building. They placed the greatest temples — including the Parthenon and the Temple of Zeus at Olympia — in the Doric order, reflecting a preference for strength and solemnity. Roman architects were bolder about mixing orders and developed the Composite capital, blending Ionic volutes with Corinthian acanthus leaves. Roman temples also typically raised the building on a high podium, so that the dramatic frontal staircase became the only point of entry — very different from Greek temples, which could be approached from all four sides.

This difference reflects a shift in the role of the building. Roman temples were often embedded in a forum or public space where the frontal view was what mattered. Greek temples, set on open hillsides or sanctuaries, were meant to be seen from all angles and were integrated into the landscape.

The Parthenon

The Parthenon, built on the Acropolis at Athens between 447 and 432 BC, is the supreme example of Doric architecture. Constructed from Pentelic marble, it measures approximately 70 metres long and 31 metres wide. Eight columns stand across each of the short ends and seventeen along each long side, creating a peristyle — a colonnade running all the way around the building. The outer columns are slightly thicker at the middle (a technique called entasis) to prevent an optical illusion of inward curvature.

Inside the cella stood the colossal chryselephantine statue of Athena Parthenos, crafted by the sculptor Pheidias. The statue was approximately 12 metres tall and made of ivory for the flesh and gold sheeting for the drapery and armour — a display of enormous wealth. The Parthenon also housed the city’s treasury and was adorned with extensive sculptural programmes: the mythological battles on the metopes, the continuous frieze around the inner colonnade, and the pedimental groups at east and west ends.

Key Fact

The Parthenon (447–432 BC) is a Doric temple on the Athenian Acropolis, dedicated to Athena. It had 8 columns on the short ends and 17 along the sides. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates; the sculptural programme was overseen by Pheidias, who also created the 12-metre ivory-and-gold cult statue inside.

The Temple of Zeus at Olympia

The Temple of Zeus at Olympia, completed around 457 BC, was one of the largest Doric temples in Greece. Built from local limestone coated in stucco, it had 6 columns at each end and 13 along each side. Inside stood another chryselephantine masterpiece by Pheidias — the seated Zeus, regarded in antiquity as one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The temple’s exterior sculptural programme was also significant: the metopes above the porch depicted the Twelve Labours of Heracles, directly connecting the sanctuary to Heracles as the founder of the Olympic Games.

Roman Temples: The Pantheon and the Temple of Fortuna Virilis

The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian around AD 125, is extraordinary because it combines a traditional Corinthian-columned porch with a vast circular rotunda. The rotunda is covered by a concrete dome 43 metres in diameter — the same measurement as its height — with a circular opening at the top called the oculus, approximately 9 metres across. Light from the oculus moves slowly across the interior throughout the day, creating an awe-inspiring effect. The Pantheon was dedicated to all the gods and has survived almost entirely intact to the present day, largely because it was converted into a Christian church in 609 AD.

The Temple of Fortuna Virilis (now identified as the Temple of Portunus), overlooking the Tiber in Rome, is one of the best-preserved Republican-era temples. Built in the late 2nd or early 1st century BC, it stands on a high podium accessed by steps at the front only. It uses the Ionic order, with four free-standing columns at the front and engaged columns (columns built into the wall) along the sides — a feature typical of Roman architecture, creating the illusion of a full colonnade while saving material and space. This engaged-column design is distinctly Roman and distinguishes it clearly from Greek peripteral temples.

Students sometimes imagine Greek and Roman temples as functioning like a church, mosque or synagogue — a space where congregations gathered inside for communal worship. This is a misconception. The cella was restricted, and the main acts of worship (sacrifice, prayer, offerings) happened outside at the altar. The interior was the god’s private home. An ancient Greek would have found the idea of a congregation sitting inside the god’s house deeply strange.

This difference matters for answering source questions: when you describe a temple, always note the relationship between the outdoor altar (where worship happened), the inner cella (where the cult statue lived), and the role of the priests who mediated between the two.

before.content_html:
Religion in Everyday Life

For the ancient Greeks and Romans, religion was not a Sunday activity or a private matter — it was woven into every aspect of daily life. Before eating, a Greek might pour a few drops of wine on the ground as a libation to the gods. Before a sea voyage, a Roman would sacrifice at a temple. When something important happened — a birth, a victory in battle, a safe return — the pious response was to honour the deity responsible. The gods were understood as active presences whose goodwill had to be maintained through regular acts of piety.

Prayer and Votive Offerings

Prayer in the ancient world had a distinctive physical dimension. Greek worshippers typically stood upright, raised their arms with palms facing upward towards the sky when addressing the Olympians, or turned them downward towards the earth when addressing gods of the underworld. Roman worshippers often covered their heads with a fold of their toga — the capite velato gesture — during prayer and sacrifice, symbolising reverence and the blocking out of bad omens.

Alongside prayer, worshippers made votive offerings. These ranged from small terracotta figurines and clay models of the body part healed (a foot, a hand, an eye) to expensive bronze tripods and silver vessels. Sanctuaries across the Greek world were filled with accumulated offerings, creating a visible record of the community’s gratitude. At the Sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, for example, stone tablets described miraculous cures, and model limbs were left in thanksgiving. The practice reflects the reciprocal logic of ancient religion: the worshipper gave something in exchange for the god’s favour.

Key Fact

Votive offerings could include terracotta figurines, model body parts, bronze vessels, weapons, jewellery or painted tablets. They expressed reciprocity — the worshipper’s side of the exchange with the deity. A fulfilled promise to dedicate an offering was called a vow in Latin; Roman temples accumulated wealth through the objects left by grateful worshippers.

Animal Sacrifice: The Central Act of Worship

Animal sacrifice was the most important and elaborate form of worship in both Greek and Roman culture. The logic was the same as with votive offerings — giving the most valuable thing possible to the gods — but sacrifice was a public, communal event that could involve hundreds of people and was closely tied to civic festivals.

In a Greek sacrifice, the animal had to be perfect and unblemished: a bull, ox, cow, sheep, goat or pig, depending on the deity and the occasion. The animal was led in procession to the altar, adorned with garlands and gilded horns for a major sacrifice. Water was sprinkled on its head, and barley grains were scattered — the animal shaking its head was interpreted as a sign of willingness. The sacrificer (who might be a priest, a magistrate, or even a general before battle) then struck the animal with an axe or stunned it before cutting its throat over the altar.

The blood was collected and poured over the altar — the altar received the god’s share. The internal organs, especially the liver and lungs, were inspected for omens (see the next lesson on divination). The thighbones were wrapped in fat and burned on the altar fire, producing the smoke that the gods were believed to find pleasing. The rest of the meat was roasted and eaten by the worshippers, making sacrifice simultaneously a religious act, a communal feast, and one of the few occasions on which ordinary Greeks ate meat.

Roman sacrifice followed a broadly similar pattern but with distinctive features. The sacrificing magistrate covered his head (capite velato) and was accompanied by specialists: a haruspex to examine the entrails, and musicians playing flutes to drown out any bad omens heard during the rite. The animals most commonly sacrificed in public Roman ritual were the bull, sheep and pig together — a ceremony known as the suovetaurilia, used for major occasions such as the purification of the army.

A critical difference: the Romans demanded absolute ritual correctness. If the priest made a mistake — mispronounced a word, broke the silence, or the animal escaped — the entire sacrifice had to be repeated from the start. This principle of piacula (atonement) meant that religious officials were extremely careful and that the procedures were highly formalised compared to Greek practice.

Key Fact

The four main stages of a Greek animal sacrifice: (1) Procession — the animal led adorned to the altar; (2) Preparation — water and barley scattered, the animal’s “consent” obtained; (3) Killing — the animal killed at the altar, blood poured over it; (4) Division — thighbones and fat burned for the gods; meat roasted and shared by the community.

Household Worship

Public sacrifice and temple ritual were not the only forms of worship. Both Greeks and Romans maintained religious practice in the home. Greek households kept a small hearth sacred to Hestia, and daily libations were poured to household gods at meals. Roman households maintained a small shrine called a lararium, where statuettes of the Lares (household guardian spirits) and the Penates (gods of the storeroom) were kept. The head of the household, the paterfamilias, conducted daily rituals at this shrine, including burning incense and offering food. This domestic piety was considered just as important as participation in public cult.

A key concept underpinning all ancient worship is the Latin phrase do ut des — “I give so that you may give.” The relationship between worshipper and deity was conceived as a reciprocal transaction: you honoured the god with prayer, sacrifice and offerings, and in return the god was expected to provide protection, good harvests, victory or health. This is very different from modern conceptions of prayer as purely spiritual or non-transactional. The gods of Greece and Rome were not morally perfect beings who demanded good behaviour from their worshippers — they wanted the correct rituals performed correctly, and regularly.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ancient Greek and Roman worship operated on a “do ut des” (give-to-receive) model: prayer, libations and votive offerings expressed piety and maintained the gods’ goodwill in return for protection and favour.
  • Animal sacrifice was the central public act of worship: the gods received the bones and fat burned on the altar fire, while the community shared the roasted meat — making sacrifice a communal feast as well as a religious rite.
  • Roman sacrifice placed greater emphasis on ritual precision (the haruspex, correct formulae, absolute silence); any error required the whole ceremony to be repeated from the beginning.

before.content_html:
The Role of Priests and Priestesses in Greece

In ancient Greece, priests and priestesses were not a professional clergy in the modern sense. A hiereus (male priest) or hiereia (female priestess) served a specific deity at a specific sanctuary. The role was often hereditary within a family, or held for a fixed term, or even purchased in some cities. Priests were not moral or spiritual advisers — their function was primarily practical: maintaining the temple, supervising the cult statue, ensuring sacrifices were performed correctly, and managing the sacred property of the sanctuary.

Priestesses played an especially important role in the cults of female deities. The priestess of Athena Polias at Athens — one of the most prestigious religious offices in the Greek world — was responsible for the care of the ancient olive-wood image of Athena on the Acropolis, a statue believed to have fallen from the sky. Priestesses of Hera and Demeter also held significant civic status, and in several cults women wielded a degree of public religious authority that was otherwise largely unavailable to them in Greek civic life.

Key Fact

Greek priests and priestesses were ritual specialists, not spiritual counsellors or moral leaders. Their essential duties were temple maintenance, correct performance of sacrifices and oversight of the sanctuary’s sacred treasures. The term hiereus (priest) and hiereia (priestess) literally relates to what is hieros — sacred or holy.

The Mantis: Prophets and Seers

Alongside priests, Greek religious life included the mantis (seer or prophet). The mantis was a specialist in reading divine signs: the flight of birds, the movement of flames in a sacrifice, the appearance of livers and lungs. Seers accompanied Greek armies in the field — no general would begin a battle without a favourable sacrifice reading. The historian Thucydides records that the Athenian general Nicias was so dependent on his seer’s readings that his paralysis during the catastrophic Sicilian Expedition of 415–413 BC contributed to the disaster.

The Oracle at Delphi

The most famous oracle in the ancient world was the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi. The sanctuary at Delphi, set high on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, was considered the omphalos — the navel of the world — where Apollo had slain the serpent Python. Cities, kings and private individuals travelled to consult Apollo’s voice at Delphi before important decisions: going to war, founding colonies, making new laws.

The oracle’s voice was the Pythia — a woman chosen from among the local people, who served as Apollo’s mouthpiece. To consult the oracle, a consultee first paid a fee and performed a preliminary sacrifice. They were then admitted to the inner sanctuary. The Pythia sat on a tripod seat above a fissure in the rock from which vapours were said to rise, inducing her trance-like state of divine inspiration. Her often ambiguous or cryptic utterances were then transmitted by the priests in verse. The most famous example of ambiguity was the response given to the Lydian king Croesus, who asked whether he should attack the Persians: Apollo’s answer was that if he crossed the river Halys, a great empire would be destroyed — which was true, though the empire destroyed was his own.

The ancient literary accounts describe the Pythia as entering an ecstatic or trance-like state, sometimes thrashing and foaming, before delivering her prophecy. Modern geological surveys of Delphi have identified intersecting fault lines beneath the sanctuary and chemical analysis has found traces of ethylene gas in the spring water — a substance that can induce hallucination in low concentrations. This has led some scholars to argue there was a genuine physical basis for the Pythia’s altered state. Others are more sceptical, noting that the accounts of violent ecstasy may be literary exaggeration and that the consultations were heavily controlled by the priests. The question of whether the Pythia was genuinely inspired or performing a religious role is a good example of the problem of using literary sources alongside archaeological evidence.

Roman Priesthoods

Roman religious authority was embedded in the structures of the state in a way that had no equivalent in Greece. The two most important priestly colleges in Republican and Imperial Rome were the pontifices and the augures. The pontifices were guardians of the religious calendar, the correct formulae for prayer and sacrifice, and the legal boundaries between sacred and secular space. Their head, the Pontifex Maximus, was one of the most powerful religious and political figures in Rome — a title later assumed by the emperors themselves. Augustus became Pontifex Maximus in 12 BC, combining supreme religious authority with supreme political power.

The augures were specialists in reading the auspices — the signs by which the gods communicated their approval or disapproval of proposed actions. No significant Roman undertaking — a battle, an election, the founding of a temple — could proceed without favourable auspices. The augur would observe a defined area of sky and report what birds appeared, in what direction, and in what numbers. An eagle flying to the right was a good omen; a raven on the left was bad. This system meant that the college of augurs had the theoretical power to veto any public action by declaring the auspices unfavourable.

Key Fact

Three key groups of Roman religious officials: (1) Pontifices — guardians of religious law and the calendar, headed by the Pontifex Maximus; (2) Augures — readers of the auspices (bird signs); (3) Haruspices — specialists in reading omens from entrails (Etruscan in origin). All three operated alongside the Vestal Virgins, who maintained Rome’s sacred flame.

The Vestal Virgins were Rome’s most celebrated priestesses, six in number, chosen between the ages of six and ten to serve Vesta — goddess of the hearth — for thirty years. Their primary duty was to maintain the sacred fire in the Aedes Vestae (Temple of Vesta) in the Roman Forum. If the fire went out, it was a terrible omen for Rome. Vestals received extraordinary privileges: they could own property, make wills and travel in public without a male guardian. Their person was legally inviolable — harming a Vestal was a capital offence. However, the penalty for breaking their vow of chastity was to be buried alive in a chamber underground. Their status illustrates the paradox of Roman women in religion: they could hold great public religious authority while being legally barred from political life.

glossary_terms.definition: A Greek male priest (hiereus) or female priestess (hiereia) responsible for the maintenance of a temple and the performance of its rituals.
A Greek female priestess who served a deity, particularly a goddess, and performed the cult's rituals on behalf of the community.
A Greek prophet or seer who interpreted omens, dreams and signs from the gods, accompanying armies and advising leaders on the divine will.
The title given to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who acted as the mouthpiece of the god, delivering oracular responses in a state of divine inspiration.
The college of Roman priests responsible for overseeing religious law, the calendar, public ceremonies and the correct performance of all state religious rites; headed by the Pontifex Maximus.
Roman priestly officials responsible for interpreting the will of the gods by observing the flight and behaviour of birds and other signs (auspices).
Divine signs interpreted by Roman augurs, especially from the behaviour and flight of birds, used to determine whether the gods approved of a proposed action.

before.content_html:
Why Did Greeks and Romans Hold Festivals?

Religious festivals in the ancient world were far more than ceremonies — they were the most elaborate and expensive public events in the calendar, combining sacrifice, procession, athletic competition, theatrical performance and communal feasting. A festival honoured a specific deity and, by doing so, reinforced the civic identity of the community hosting it. Athenians celebrated the Panathenaia not just as religious piety but as an assertion of Athenian greatness — and in this way myth, religion and civic politics were inseparable.

The Great Panathenaia

The Panathenaia was Athens’ most important civic festival, held annually in the summer month of Hekatombaion, with a grander “Great” Panathenaia every four years. The centrepiece was a grand procession that climbed the Acropolis from the city below. The key moment was the delivery of the peplos — a large woven robe depicting the Gigantomachy — to the ancient olive-wood statue of Athena Polias on the Acropolis. This robe was carried up on the mast of a ship mounted on wheels, rolled through the city streets.

The procession itself is immortalised in one of the greatest surviving works of classical art: the Parthenon frieze. Running around all four sides of the inner colonnade of the Parthenon, the frieze carved in low relief shows a continuous procession of horsemen, chariots, musicians, sacrificial animals (cattle and sheep), water-carriers and maidens, culminating in the presentation of the peplos to Athena. The frieze is approximately 160 metres long and was carved under the direction of Pheidias in the 440s BC. It is now divided between the Acropolis Museum in Athens and the British Museum in London.

Key Fact

The Parthenon frieze (carved c. 440s BC) depicts the Panathenaic procession. Running approximately 160 metres around the inner colonnade of the Parthenon, it shows horsemen, chariots, cattle, maidens and the presentation of the peplos to Athena. It is divided between the Acropolis Museum, Athens, and the British Museum, London.

The City Dionysia

The City Dionysia was held each spring in honour of Dionysus, the god of wine, fertility and transformation. The festival lasted several days and included a grand procession, sacrifices, and most famously the performance of tragic and comic plays in competitive contests at the Theatre of Dionysus on the southern slope of the Acropolis. Three tragedians each presented three tragedies and a satyr play over three days of competition, with a panel of judges awarding prizes. Comic poets competed separately.

Attending the City Dionysia was a civic duty as much as an entertainment. Citizens were expected to attend; admission was either free or subsidised by the state for those who could not afford it. The performances were a form of religious worship — the theatre of Dionysus contained a priest’s throne of honour — but they were also a space where Athenian society debated its values, challenged its assumptions and explored its fears. The great tragedians whose works survive — Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides — all won prizes at the City Dionysia.

Greek tragedy and comedy grew from choral performances in honour of Dionysus — the word “tragedy” may derive from tragos (goat) and ode (song), perhaps reflecting an early ritual involving a goat sacrifice or a goat-costumed chorus. By the 5th century BC the connection to ritual was structural: the theatre was sacred space, the priest of Dionysus had the central honorary seat, and the performances were part of a multi-day religious celebration. Students sometimes separate “Greek drama” from “Greek religion” — they should not. For an Athenian, watching Sophocles’ Antigone was a religious experience.

Roman Festivals: Lupercalia and Saturnalia

Roman religious festivals were equally numerous and varied. The Lupercalia, held on 15 February, was one of Rome’s oldest and strangest festivals. It began with the sacrifice of goats and a dog in the cave of the Lupercal — the cave on the Palatine Hill where, according to legend, the she-wolf had suckled Romulus and Remus. Priests called Luperci then ran near-naked in two bands around the Palatine Hill, striking people they met with strips cut from the skins of the sacrificed animals. Women who were struck were believed to become fertile. The festival was directly connected to the foundation myth of Rome and to ideas of purification.

The Saturnalia was celebrated in December in honour of Saturn, the god of agriculture and the harvest. It lasted several days and was characterised by a deliberate inversion of social norms: masters waited on their slaves at table, gambling in public was temporarily permitted, and gifts were exchanged. The atmosphere was one of carnival licence. The Saturnalia was enormously popular and its customs clearly influenced later mid-winter festivities in the Roman Empire and beyond.

Key Fact

The Saturnalia (December) was a festival of Saturn in which social hierarchy was temporarily overturned: masters waited on slaves, gifts were exchanged, and public licence was permitted. This ritual inversion was controlled — it reinforced the normal hierarchy by making its reversal a temporary holiday rather than a permanent change.

The great Greek festivals were not only local events. The Olympic Games, held every four years at Olympia in honour of Zeus, drew competitors from across the Greek world and even declared a sacred truce (ekecheiria) during which wars were suspended. Similarly, the Great Panathenaia attracted participants from Athens’ subject allies throughout the Aegean. Hosting a magnificent festival was a demonstration of power as well as piety. The Athenian general Pericles used the rebuilding of the Acropolis and the grandeur of the Panathenaia to assert Athenian supremacy over the Delian League. In this way, festivals were inseparable from the political ambitions of the city.

Why Burial Mattered

For ancient Greeks and Romans, proper burial was not a formality — it was a religious and moral necessity. The unburied dead were believed to wander the banks of the underworld rivers, unable to cross into the realm of Hades until their body had received the correct rites. Sophocles’ tragedy Antigone turns on this very point: Antigone defies the king’s edict in order to bury her brother, because leaving him unburied would condemn his soul to restless wandering. The obligation to bury the dead — and to bury them correctly — was one of the most powerful moral imperatives in the ancient world.

Greek Funeral Customs: The Prothesis

The Greek funeral followed a set sequence of three stages. The first was the prothesis — the laying-out of the body. Once someone died, the women of the household washed the body, anointed it with oil, dressed it in grave clothes, and placed it on a bier or low table in the entrance hall of the house, with the feet pointing towards the door. The body was wreathed with garlands. Family and friends gathered to lament, with women performing formal ritualised mourning — wailing, beating their breasts and tearing their hair. Athens eventually passed laws limiting the extremes of this mourning behaviour, suggesting it had become a competitive display of grief among wealthy families.

Evidence for the prothesis comes from surviving painted pottery. Attic geometric-period pottery from the 8th century BC shows schematic but unmistakeable scenes of the prothesis: the body laid horizontally on a bier, surrounded by rows of stylised mourning figures, with arms raised in the gesture of lamentation. These vessels were themselves often grave goods, placed in the tomb alongside the deceased.

Key Fact

The three stages of a Greek funeral: (1) Prothesis — the preparation and laying-out of the body in the home; (2) Ekphora — the funeral procession to the place of burial or cremation; (3) Burial or cremation — the body interred in the earth or burned on a pyre, with grave goods.

The Ekphora and Burial

The second stage was the ekphora — the funeral procession. It took place before dawn, a rule probably intended to prevent excessive public display. The body, on its bier, was carried or transported on a cart to the burial ground, which lay outside the city walls — death was ritually impure and had to be kept apart from the living community. Male relatives walked in the procession; female mourners were often (in Athenian law) restricted to those over sixty or close family, again reflecting attempts to control the scale of display.

The body could be either buried in the earth or cremated, depending on period and local custom. Grave goods — pottery, jewellery, weapons, figurines — were placed in the tomb to accompany the dead. Graves were often marked above ground by stone stelai or sculpted monuments. The stele (plural stelai) typically bore the deceased’s name and sometimes a relief carving. Some of the finest examples survive from classical Athens: the Hegeso Stele (now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens) shows a seated woman receiving a jewellery box from a standing female attendant, rendered with quiet elegance and carved in relief.

A widely attested Greek and Roman practice was placing a coin in the mouth or on the eyes of the deceased. This coin was the fare for Charon, the ferryman who transported souls across the river Styx (or Acheron) to the underworld. Without this payment, the soul could not cross and would be left to wander the bank for a hundred years. Archaeological evidence — coins found in graves in both the Greek and Roman worlds — confirms the literary accounts. The practice is vivid evidence of how Greek and Roman beliefs about the soul’s journey after death shaped funerary behaviour.

Greek Festivals for the Dead: Genesia

The dead were not forgotten after burial. The Genesia was an Athenian public festival in honour of the dead and the ancestors, held annually. Offerings of food and libations were brought to the graves, and the family commemorated their dead together. Private family commemoration of the dead also took place on the third day after death (the trita) and the ninth day (the enata).

Roman Funeral Practices

Roman funerals closely paralleled their Greek counterparts in structure but had distinctively Roman features. The body was washed and prepared by the family, but wealthy Romans could belong to funeral clubs (collegia funeraticia), which guaranteed a proper burial for members who could not afford one independently. The funeral procession in Rome was often elaborate: for a noble Roman, professional mourners (praeficae) were hired, musicians played, and actors wearing the death masks (imagines) of the deceased’s ancestors walked in the procession, creating a living tableau of the family’s lineage.

Roman burial law required interment outside city walls, and the major roads leading out of Rome — especially the Via Appia — were lined with tombs, mausoleums and grave monuments. Romans used both burial and cremation, with cremation becoming fashionable among the elite during the Imperial period before inhumation (burial) returned to favour in the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, partly under the influence of Eastern religions and later Christianity.

Key Fact

The Parentalia (13–21 February) was a period of private commemoration of dead family members, when temples closed, marriages were forbidden, and families visited graves with offerings. The Lemuria (9, 11 and 13 May) was a festival to appease the lemures — restless, potentially harmful spirits of the dead — through a midnight ritual performed by the paterfamilias.

Both cultures shared the belief that the dead required ongoing attention and offerings — neglecting the dead was dangerous as well as impious. The Greek Genesia and the Roman Parentalia served the same basic function: keeping the dead appeased through annual ritual. However, the Roman Lemuria suggests a stronger anxiety about potentially malevolent spirits of the dead returning to harm the living — a belief with no clear Greek parallel at the same level of elaboration. The Roman use of ancestor masks (imagines) in funerary processions was also distinctively Roman, serving the political function of displaying the family’s social prestige and distinguished history.

practice_questions.text: What is the Greek term for the funeral procession that carried the body from the home to the burial ground?
Describe the prothesis stage of a Greek funeral.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the body was washed and anointed with oil by the women of the household; the body was dressed in grave clothes and laid out on a bier in the entrance hall; the feet pointed towards the door; the body was wreathed with garlands; family and friends gathered to lament; women performed formal ritualised mourning (wailing, beating breasts, tearing hair); the prothesis took place in the home before the ekphora.

practice_questions.text: Consider this description of a carved stone grave monument: a tall stone slab carved in shallow relief, showing a seated woman dressed in elegant drapery who reaches towards an open jewellery box held out to her by a standing female figure; below the scene the woman's name is inscribed. What does this monument tell us about Greek attitudes towards death and commemoration? Use specific details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Uses multiple specific details (seated woman = the deceased shown in a moment of ordinary life; standing attendant = her slave, suggesting status; jewellery box = personal identity and wealth; shallow relief carving = refined craft honouring the dead; inscribed name = public commemoration of the individual) with sustained analysis of what each implies about Greek attitudes (the desire to remember the dead as they were in life; the importance of status; the role of women in maintaining social memory; the stele as public statement); clear judgement.
Secure (3-4): Two or three details analysed with explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description without engaging with source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why proper burial was so important in ancient Greek and Roman culture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: the unburied dead were believed unable to cross into Hades, condemned to wander for a hundred years; the obligation to bury was a moral and religious duty on the family; without a coin for Charon the soul could not cross the underworld rivers; proper burial kept the dead from becoming restless spirits who might harm the living; burial rites maintained the family's social prestige and public identity; it is illustrated in Sophocles' Antigone where Antigone defies a king's order to ensure her brother's burial.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Greek and Roman approaches to death and burial were essentially the same? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument identifying genuine similarities (both required burial outside city walls; both had ritual laying-out of the body; both used grave goods; both had festivals for the dead; both placed coins for Charon) alongside real differences (Roman funeral clubs for the poor with no Greek equivalent; Roman use of ancestor masks in processions; Lemuria specifically for malevolent spirits vs Genesia for honoured ancestors; Roman cremation was an elite fashion linked to Imperial period; stelai in Greece vs elaborate roadside tombs and mausoleums in Rome); evidence from named sources (Sophocles' Antigone, the Hegeso Stele, Parentalia and Lemuria); clear judgement.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with evidence for similarities and differences and a conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Points about one side with limited comparison or source use.
Emerging (1-2): Descriptive account; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Roman festivals for the dead differed from the Greek festival of the Genesia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Lemuria aimed at appeasing potentially harmful lemures/spirits vs Genesia as a respectful commemoration of honoured ancestors; Parentalia as a private family event with public ceremonies at graves vs Genesia as a public festival; Roman civic dimension of the Parentalia with public ceremonies and closure of temples vs Genesia as primarily a family affair; the duration of Parentalia — nine days — vs the Genesia which was a single-day event) each with named evidence and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about Roman vs Greek attitudes to the dead.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek funerals followed three stages — prothesis (laying-out), ekphora (procession) and burial or cremation — with ongoing commemoration at the Genesia festival and at family anniversaries; stelai marked graves and served as a public record of the deceased.
  • The custom of placing a coin in the mouth or on the eyes of the dead reflects belief in Charon, the ferryman of the underworld, and reveals how burial rites were directly shaped by beliefs about the soul’s journey after death.
  • Roman festivals for the dead — the Parentalia (February, for family commemoration) and the Lemuria (May, to appease restless spirits) — show that the Roman dead required ongoing ritual attention; the use of ancestor masks in noble funerary processions linked the individual death to the family’s political identity and public prestige.

glossary_terms.definition: The first stage of a Greek funeral: the preparation and public laying-out of the body in the home, with the family gathering to mourn around it.
The second stage of a Greek funeral: the procession that carried the body from the home to the place of burial or cremation, typically held before dawn.
An upright stone grave marker, often inscribed with the name of the deceased and sometimes carved with a relief scene showing the person in life.
In Greek myth, the ferryman of the dead who transported souls across the river Styx (or Acheron) to the underworld, requiring payment of a coin placed in the mouth or on the eyes of the deceased.
An Athenian annual public festival held in honour of the dead and the ancestors, at which offerings were made at graves.
Roman associations whose members paid regular dues to guarantee a proper funeral and burial for themselves and their families, particularly among the poor and slave populations.
